lesson.title: The age and afterglow of the Big Bang

steps.headline: Run the expansion backwards and every galaxy set off 1/H₀ ago.

lead.text: If each galaxy had always receded at its present speed, one at distance d set off a time d ÷ v ago. Since v = H₀d, the d cancels: the time is 1/H₀, the same for every galaxy. This is the expansion age.

steps.headline: Find 1/H₀ in billions of years for H₀ = 60 km/s per Mpc.

workedSteps.text: Write 1 Mpc in kilometres, so the kilometres cancel.
Divide by the seconds in a billion years.

lead.text: Same method with H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc. Use 1 Mpc = 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km and 1 billion years = 3.156 × 10¹⁶ s.

reveal.text: About 14 billion years. Careful modelling of the changing expansion gives 13.8 billion years, so this simple estimate is close.

steps.headline: A hot, dense early universe leaves a cold, uniform glow: the cosmic microwave background.

lead.text: In 1965 Penzias and Wilson found faint microwave radiation arriving equally from every direction. Its spectrum is an almost perfect blackbody at 2.725 K, just what a universe that was once hot and dense should leave behind.
Wien's law applies as before: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K ÷ T. Give the answer in millimetres.

reveal.text: A peak near a millimetre lies in the microwave range, which is how the background got its name.

lead.text: About 380,000 years after the Big Bang the universe had cooled to about 3,000 K, cool enough for electrons to join nuclei into neutral atoms. Light then travelled freely. Since then expansion has stretched every wavelength, and the temperature has fallen in step.

reveal.text: Every wavelength has grown about a thousand-fold. Glow that left as visible and infrared light now arrives as microwaves.

lead.text: The age estimate is inversely proportional to H₀. Use 1/H₀ = 977.8 billion years ÷ H₀, which has the unit conversion built in.

reveal.text: A smaller H₀ means slower expansion, so the galaxies took longer to get where they are. Stars older than 1/H₀ would be a contradiction.

lesson.orientation: Estimate the age of the universe from H₀ and read its early heat in the microwave background.
lesson.reviewLabel: The age and afterglow of the Big Bang

blocks.text: A car is now 100 km from your door, driving straight away from it at a steady 50 km/h. It started from the door.

intro.promise: By the end you'll estimate the universe's age from H₀ and say what the microwave background tells us.

recap.keyIdea: Running the expansion backwards gives 1/H₀, about 14 billion years. The early universe's heat survives as the microwave background, a 2.725 K blackbody stretched about 1,100 times.

blocks.text: You found that a car driving away at 50 km/h from 100 km out left 2 hours ago, that H₀ = 70 gives 14.0 billion years, and that the background's wavelengths have grown 1,101 times.

recap.nextHook: That completes the course, from the turning sky to the afterglow of the Big Bang.

questions.prompt: With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, 1 Mpc = 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km and 1 billion years = 3.156 × 10¹⁶ s, find 1/H₀ in billions of years, to one decimal place.
hints: Write H₀ as 70 km/s per 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km so the kilometres cancel.
Divide 3.086 × 10¹⁹ by 70 to get seconds.
Convert seconds to billions of years.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1/H₀ = 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km ÷ 70 km/s = 4.409 × 10¹⁷ s; ÷ 3.156 × 10¹⁶ s = 13.97, about 14.0 billion years.

questions.onCorrect: 14.0 billion years. 1/H₀ is a Mpc in km divided by H₀, converted to years.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in seconds. Divide by 3.156 × 10¹⁶ to get billions of years.

questions.prompt: The cosmic microwave background is a blackbody at 2.725 K. Using λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / T, find its peak wavelength in millimetres, to two decimal places.
hints: Divide Wien's constant by the temperature.
The result is in metres.
Multiply by 1,000 to convert to millimetres.
questions.onCorrect: 1.06 mm. Wien's law gives metres; multiply by 1,000 for millimetres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in metres. Multiply by 1,000 to turn it into millimetres.

questions.prompt: The cosmic background was released at about 3,000 K and is now 2.725 K. By what factor have its wavelengths been stretched since then, to the nearest whole number?
hints: Wien's law makes peak wavelength inversely proportional to temperature.
So the stretch factor is the ratio of the two temperatures.
Divide the earlier temperature by today's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Temperature falls as wavelengths stretch, so the factor is 3,000/2.725 = 1,100.9, which is 1,101 to the nearest whole number.

questions.onCorrect: 1,101. Wavelengths stretch in the same proportion as the temperature falls.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down. The wavelengths grew, so the factor is above one.

questions.prompt: Using 1/H₀ = 977.8 billion years ÷ H₀ (H₀ in km/s per Mpc), find 1/H₀ for H₀ = 50, in billions of years, to one decimal place.
hints: The constant 977.8 converts the units for you.
Divide it by the value of H₀.
Round to one decimal place.
questions.onCorrect: 19.6 billion years. A smaller H₀ means slower expansion and a longer time.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides H₀ by the constant. Divide the constant by H₀.

questions.prompt: What kind of spectrum does the cosmic microwave background have? Answer with the one-word name for the spectrum of an ideal thermal emitter.
hints: It is the same kind of spectrum Wien's law describes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A blackbody spectrum, the closest to perfect ever measured, at 2.725 K.

questions.onCorrect: Blackbody: the closest to a perfect thermal spectrum ever measured, at 2.725 K.

misconceptions.feedback: Microwave says where it peaks. The question asks for the kind of spectrum, the ideal thermal one.

questions.prompt: Why is 1/H₀ only an approximation to the age of the universe?
hints: What does 1/H₀ assume about each galaxy's speed?

acceptedIdeas: The expansion rate has changed over time, slowed by gravity and later sped up
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 1/H₀ assumes each galaxy kept a constant speed. Gravity slowed the early expansion and dark energy has since accelerated it; the two effects nearly cancel, so 13.8 billion years is close to 1/H₀.

choices.label: The expansion rate has changed over time, slowed by gravity and later sped up
Light from distant galaxies travelled faster than light does now
Galaxies only recede from the Milky Way, so the formula ignores the rest

questions.onCorrect: 1/H₀ assumes a constant speed for each galaxy, but the expansion rate has changed over time.

misconceptions.feedback: Light has travelled at the same speed throughout. Look at what 1/H₀ assumes about each galaxy's speed.
Galaxies recede from every other galaxy too. Look at what 1/H₀ assumes about each galaxy's speed.

questions.prompt: How many hours ago did it leave?
hints: Time is distance divided by speed.
Put in 100 km and 50 km/h.
Divide 100 by 50.
questions.onCorrect: 2 hours. A steady speed gives time = distance ÷ speed, the same logic that dates the expansion.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies distance and speed. Time is distance divided by speed.
That divides speed by distance. Time is distance divided by speed.

questions.prompt: A galaxy twice as far away has twice the speed. How does its time since leaving compare?
hints: Time is distance ÷ speed.
questions.onCorrect: Distance and speed both double, so d ÷ v is unchanged: the time is the same for every galaxy.

misconceptions.feedback: The distance doubles, but so does the speed. Time is distance ÷ speed, so look at the ratio.
The speed doubles, but so does the distance. Time is distance ÷ speed, so look at the ratio.

hints: Write H₀ as km/s per (3.086 × 10¹⁹ km).

acceptedIdeas: H₀ is in km/s per Mpc, and the Mpc has been written in km.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: H₀ is in km/s per Mpc, and the Mpc has been written in km.

choices.label: H₀ is in km/s per Mpc, and the Mpc has been written in km.

questions.onCorrect: H₀ is a speed per distance, so with the distance in km the kilometres divide out and leave 1/seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: The size of a kilometre does not matter. The units divide out.
They do: km/s per km leaves 1/s, and its reciprocal is a time.

questions.prompt: Where does the cosmic microwave background arrive from?
hints: It fills space, left over from the early universe.

choices.label: Only the centre of the Milky Way
Only the direction of the Sun

questions.onCorrect: The glow fills all of space, so it arrives from every direction with almost the same strength.

misconceptions.feedback: The background is not tied to any one object in our galaxy. It fills space.
The Sun is far too local a source. The background comes from the whole early universe.

questions.prompt: Light of wavelength 1.0 µm set out when the glow was released. Stretched by a factor of 1,101 since then, what is its wavelength now, in millimetres, to two decimal places?
hints: Multiply the wavelength by the stretch factor.
That gives micrometres.
Divide by 1,000 to convert micrometres to millimetres.
questions.onCorrect: 1.10 mm. Stretching by 1,101 turns near-infrared light into microwaves.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the length in micrometres. Divide by 1,000 to get millimetres.
